A study of adolescents’ social media use reported that most participants experienced no short-term changes in well-being related to social media; among those who did experience changes, positive changes were more common than negative ones. Individual effects ranged from tiny or small to moderate or strong, even though overall effects were small. The authors suggested that averaging across adolescents with different susceptibilities may explain why earlier research often found small or no effects.
records.topic: individual differences in social media effects

records.text: The study distinguished active from passive social media use and found different associations with adolescents’ affective well-being. On average, passive use of Instagram and WhatsApp appeared to enhance adolescents’ well-being, contrasting with findings among adults that passive Facebook use was associated with lower affective well-being. The authors proposed enjoyment, humorous content or memes, and positive feedback as possible explanations for improvements, while envy might help explain declines for some adolescents.
records.topic: active and passive social media use

records.text: In the study, time spent passively using WhatsApp was associated with improved well-being, and this association did not differ between adolescents. The association between passive Instagram use and well-being varied between adolescents. The authors suggested that WhatsApp’s more private, mostly one-to-one communication may elicit more homogeneous responses, whereas Instagram’s public mix of friends, celebrities, influencers, intimate communication, self-presentation, and social comparison may elicit varied or opposing responses such as envy and inspiration.

A figure in the study showed dose–response associations between passive Instagram use, measured in minutes per hour, and affective well-being for 46 adolescents. Red lines indicated significant negative within-person associations, green lines significant positive associations, and gray lines nonsignificant associations. The figure included participants who completed at least 10 assessments; 13 were excluded for completing fewer than 10 assessments, and one was excluded because passive Instagram use was constant across assessments.

The study’s participants were relatively happy overall, and its findings may not generalize to clinical samples or young people with lower social-emotional well-being. The study measured affective well-being as happiness, not other forms such as cognitive well-being. The authors called for research to identify adolescents particularly susceptible to declines, including investigation of whether negative feedback might be involved.

The study’s authors recommended follow-up measures and longer-term research beyond a one-week experience-sampling study to determine whether momentary associations between social media use and adolescent affective well-being accumulate into lasting consequences, including among adolescents who show no short-term changes.

The study’s authors recommended distinguishing more precisely among social media activities, including passive private use such as reading WhatsApp messages or Instagram direct messages and passive public use such as browsing an Instagram feed, to clarify how specific activities relate to well-being.
records.topic: future research on social media activities
